me_beech_cliff_bouldering.blurb: A boulder field on the upper slopes of Beech Mountain, on the quieter western half of Mount Desert Island in Acadia National Park. The 26 problems are almost all bouldering, with a single top rope. Grades cluster around V3 and V4 with plenty of easy and moderate lines below, then thin out into a few hard problems near the top end, plus one 5.12 top-rope line. Blocks start near the trailhead lot and are scattered along the valley path heading south, so expect to wander and read the trails carefully. A good pick for a mixed group where some want warm-ups and others want something serious.

me_strip_boulder.blurb: One long boulder within the South Freeport boulders, a short drive north of Portland. All 24 problems are bouldering, ranging from easy lines through a solid middle of V3 to V5, with a handful around V6 and a single problem near V9 for the strong. Reach it by following the road up from the pullout past several roadside blocks, then taking the path uphill into the woods and passing the big prow known as the Coffin. The approach is brief, so it fits an after-work session. Expect slab and sloper style climbing on sharp stone.

me_canada_cliff_boulder.blurb: The boulders beneath Canada Cliff, up the hill from the Echo Lake parking lot in Acadia National Park. The 23 problems span the full range: a few very easy warm-ups, a strong core between V2 and V4, and several hard lines up to roughly V11. Most of the climbing is on the main boulder and the Shark Tooth boulder, with lip traverses and arete lines among the favorites. The setting is wooded and sheltered from wind, which suits summer and fall visits, and one tall problem has an awkward landing, so bring pads and spotters.

me_natanis_perch.blurb: The biggest of the cliffs at Chain of Ponds in the Western Mountains, sitting on a hillside above Natanis Pond along Route 27. Granite rises to roughly 200 feet, and the 22 routes are nearly all traditional, one or two pitches long, following cracks from thin fingers to wide. Grades run from about 5.6 up to 5.11, with the bulk in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, and a couple of bolted lines where gear is scarce. The feel is remote and scenic, a good fit for climbers who like quiet, less visited crags.
me_natanis_perch.parking_note: Leave the car at the signed highway overlook above Natanis Pond on Route 27; the trail to the cliff begins from there.

me_main_face_2.blurb: The central stretch of Shagg Crag, a steep granite cliff in Maine's Western Mountains near Woodstock. All 22 routes here are sport climbs, and the wall is known for powerful, juggy, sustained climbing. Almost everything is hard: a dozen routes sit in the 5.12s and several more in the 5.13s, with just a couple of easier lines to warm up on. It makes a strong choice for endurance-minded climbers working at or near their limit, and the hike in is long enough that you will want a full day planned.

me_sunset_hill.blurb: A compact bouldering spot in the Bangor area, tucked among cabins on a hillside with a short walk from the lot. Most of the 22 problems are on a broken band of rock roughly 14 to 25 feet high, and the mix includes cracks, roofs and some highball lines. The grades are friendly: most climbs are V0 or V1, with a few at V2 to V4 and one trad line. Bring several crash pads and a spotter, since a few of the taller problems have serious landings. Good for beginners and for quick sessions.
